represented a major step forward. While still centralized, CVS operated on entire
intent (self-declared):
diagram…
projects rather than individual files. More importantly, CVS introduced optimistic
locking—instead of preventing concurrent access, CVS allowed multiple developers to
work on the same file simultaneously. When they tried to commit their changes, CVS
would attempt to merge them automatically. If the changes didn't overlap, the merge
would succeed. If they did conflict, the developer would be notified and could resolve
the conflict manually.
This shift from pessimistic to optimistic concurrency was philosophically important.
It reflected a more accurate understanding of how software development actually works:
most changes don't conflict, and preventing access to files based on the assumption of
conflict is unnecessarily restrictive. CVS became widely adopted and remained the
dominant version control system for many years, particularly in open-source projects.
CVS introduced several other important features that became standard: the ability to
branch development, tagging releases, and checking out arbitrary versions. However,
CVS had limitations. It was centralized, meaning all operations required communication
with a central server. Network latency could be problematic, and the central
repository was a single point of failure. Additionally, CVS's approach to merging,
while innovative for its time, was relatively primitive. Moving branches and tags was
